title: The Three Baskets
bigQuestion: How are the Buddhist scriptures organized, and why is there no single Buddhist Bible?

story.title: Three Baskets on a Shelf
story.kicker: A monk explains why the old books were once stored in three baskets.
paragraphs: A fourth-grade class visits a Theravada Buddhist temple near Chicago. A monk in an orange robe greets them at the door. He bows slightly with his palms together. The students bow back.
He leads them to a wooden shelf. On it sit rows of books with gold letters. "These are our scriptures," he says. "We call them the Tipitaka. That means three baskets."

A boy named Omar raises his hand. "Why baskets?" The monk smiles. "Long ago, in India, workers passed dirt and bricks along in baskets. Some teachers say the name came from that. Others say the palm-leaf books were kept in baskets. Either way, the teachings were sorted into three groups."
He holds up three fingers. "One basket is for rules for monks and nuns. One is for the Buddha's talks. One is for careful lists about the mind." The students count along with him.
Omar looks at the long shelf. "That is a lot of books," he says. The monk nods. "And this is only one part of the Buddhist library." The students look around the room with new eyes.
story.think: Why might a big collection of teachings be sorted into groups?

lessons.title: Three Baskets in Pali
lessons.mainIdea: The Tipitaka, or three baskets, is the collection of scriptures Theravada Buddhists use, written in the Pali language.
reading: Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos share one big set of scriptures. It is called the *Tipitaka*. The word means "three baskets." Tipitaka is the Pali form. The Sanskrit form is Tripitaka.

The Tipitaka is written in *Pali*. Pali is an old language from India. Few people speak it at home today. Monks learn it to read and chant the texts. English readers often call this collection the Pali Canon.

Buddhists believe the Tipitaka holds the Buddha's teachings as his students remembered them. Scholars say it grew over several centuries. Both groups agree it is very old and very large. The English translation fills dozens of books.

words.d: "three baskets"; the collection of scriptures in the Pali language
an old language of India used for Theravada Buddhist scriptures

look.title: The Three Baskets
look.unit: basket number, in the usual order
look.cite: The Pali Tipitaka, Pali Text Society editions (1877 onward)

check.q: What does Tipitaka mean?
check.why: Tipitaka is a Pali word meaning three baskets.

check.q: What language is the Tipitaka written in?
check.why: The Theravada scriptures are in Pali, an old language of India.

check.q: Which Buddhists use the Pali Tipitaka as their main scripture?
check.why: Theravada Buddhists in countries like Thailand and Sri Lanka use the Pali Canon.

lessons.title: The Vinaya Basket
lessons.mainIdea: The Vinaya holds the rules for Buddhist monks and nuns and stories of why each rule was made.
reading: The first basket is the *Vinaya*. It holds the rules for monks and nuns. The rules cover eating, clothing, sleeping and living together. They also explain how to settle arguments.

Each rule comes with a story. The Vinaya tells what happened, and then how the Buddha made a rule about it. For example, it tells of monks traveling in the rainy season. Farmers worried about their crops being stepped on. So monks were asked to stay in one place during the rains.
Theravada monks recite the main list of rules together twice a month. This list is called the *Patimokkha*. For fully ordained monks it has 227 rules. Nuns have a longer list.

words.d: the basket of rules for Buddhist monks and nuns
the main list of monastic rules, recited twice a month

look.title: A Rule With a Story
look.text: A class makes a rule: "Push in your chair." Why? Last week someone tripped over one. The Vinaya works the same way. Each rule comes with the story of what happened first.
look.prompt: Why might it help to know the story behind a rule?

check.q: What is in the Vinaya?
check.why: The Vinaya is the basket of monastic rules.

check.q: How many rules are on the Theravada monks' main list?
check.why: The Theravada Patimokkha for monks has 227 rules. 423 is the number of Dhammapada verses.

check.q: Why do monks stay in one place during the rains, says the Vinaya?
choices: so they would not trample crops
check.why: The Vinaya says farmers worried about crops, so monks stayed put in the rainy season.

lessons.title: The Sutta and Abhidhamma Baskets
lessons.mainIdea: The Sutta basket holds the Buddha's talks, and the Abhidhamma basket holds careful lists about the mind.
reading: The second basket is the Sutta basket. A *sutta* is a talk or teaching. The Sanskrit word is sutra. Most suttas show the Buddha or a student teaching someone. There are thousands of them.
The suttas are grouped into five collections called Nikayas. Some hold long talks. Some hold middle-length talks. One, the Khuddaka Nikaya, holds a mix of shorter books.

The third basket is the *Abhidhamma*. It sorts ideas about the mind into careful lists. It names kinds of thoughts and feelings. Theravada teachers value it highly. Many scholars think it was put together later than the suttas.

words.d: a talk or teaching of the Buddha (Sanskrit: sutra)
the basket of careful lists and explanations about the mind

look.title: The Five Nikayas
look.cite: Pali Canon Sutta Pitaka, common counts; Khuddaka Nikaya not counted here
look.prompt: Which collection has the fewest suttas? Why might that be?

check.q: What is a sutta?
check.why: A sutta is a talk or teaching, usually by the Buddha or a student.

check.q: What is the Abhidhamma about?
check.why: The Abhidhamma sorts ideas about the mind into lists.

check.q: What is the Sanskrit form of sutta?
check.why: Sutta is the Pali form and sutra the Sanskrit form.

lessons.title: The Dhammapada
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada is a short book of 423 verses inside the Sutta basket.
reading: The *Dhammapada* sits in the Khuddaka Nikaya, the collection of shorter books. Its name means something like "path of the teaching." It has 423 short verses in 26 chapters.
Many Buddhists memorize its verses. They are short and easy to remember, like proverbs. Chapters have names like "The Mind," "Flowers" and "Anger." Readers often quote them.
The Dhammapada is one of the best-known Buddhist books in the world. It has been translated into many languages. One of the first English translations was by F. Max Muller in 1881.

words.d: a book of 423 short verses in the Pali Canon
a short numbered piece of a sacred text

look.title: The Dhammapada's First Verse
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
look.cite: Dhammapada 1, tr. F. Max Muller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: In your own words, what does this verse say comes first?

check.q: How many verses are in the Dhammapada?
check.why: The Dhammapada has 423 verses. It has 26 chapters.

check.q: Which basket holds the Dhammapada?
check.why: The Dhammapada is in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta basket.

check.q: Who made an early English translation in 1881?
check.why: F. Max Muller translated the Dhammapada in 1881.

lessons.title: The Jatakas
lessons.mainIdea: The Jatakas, stories of the Buddha's earlier lives, are also in the Sutta basket.
reading: The Khuddaka Nikaya also holds the *Jatakas*. These are stories Buddhists tell about the Buddha's earlier lives. There are about 547 of them. The stories are often long.
In the Pali Canon itself, each Jataka is a set of verses. A later commentary tells the full story around the verses. Most people know the stories from that commentary.
The last ten Jatakas are long and famous. The very last is the story of Prince Vessantara, who gives away everything he has. Buddhists in Thailand and Laos still hear it told at festivals.

words.d: a story of one of the Buddha's earlier lives
a later book that explains an older text

look.title: Verses and Story
look.text: In the canon, the Hare Jataka is a few short verses. The commentary adds the four friends, the traveler and the moon. The verses are the heart. The story is the body around it.
look.prompt: Why might a teacher add a story around a few verses?

check.q: About how many Jatakas are there?
check.why: The Pali collection has about 547 Jatakas.

check.q: What is a commentary?
choices: a later book that explains an older text
check.why: A commentary explains an older text. The Jataka stories come mostly from one.

check.q: Who is the hero of the last Jataka?
check.why: The last Jataka tells of Prince Vessantara's giving.

lessons.title: "Thus Have I Heard"
lessons.mainIdea: Suttas usually begin "Thus have I heard," words tradition gives to the Buddha's student Ananda.
reading: Many suttas begin the same way: "Thus have I heard." In Pali it is *evam me sutam*. Then the sutta names a place. It might say the Buddha was staying in a park near a city.
Buddhist tradition says the "I" is Ananda. He was the Buddha's cousin and helper. He was known for his memory. Tradition says he recited the suttas after the Buddha died.
The opening tells listeners where a teaching came from. It says, in effect, "I did not make this up. I heard it." Mahayana sutras start the same way. It also marks the start.

words.d: the Buddha's cousin and helper, remembered for his memory
Pali for "Thus have I heard," the usual opening of a sutta

look.title: How a Sutta Opens
look.text: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying near a city, in a park given by a friend.
look.cite: The standard opening of Pali suttas (e.g., Digha Nikaya 16), paraphrased
look.prompt: What two things does this opening tell the listener?

check.q: How do many suttas begin?
check.why: Suttas usually open with "Thus have I heard," evam me sutam.

check.q: Who does tradition say the "I" is?
check.why: Buddhist tradition says Ananda recited the suttas.

check.q: Why does the opening matter?
choices: it tells where the teaching came from
check.why: The opening says the speaker heard the teaching, not made it up.

lessons.title: Mahayana Sutras
lessons.mainIdea: Mahayana Buddhists also treasure many other sutras, first written in Sanskrit and kept in Chinese and Tibetan.
reading: *Mahayana* Buddhism is followed in China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and Tibet. Mahayana means "great vehicle." Mahayana Buddhists honor many early texts too. They also treasure many other sutras.

Famous ones include the Lotus Sutra, the Heart Sutra and the Diamond Sutra. Many were first written in Sanskrit. Many Sanskrit copies were later lost. They survive in Chinese and Tibetan translations.
Mahayana Buddhists believe these sutras teach the Buddha's deepest message. Scholars date most of them from about the 1st century BCE onward. Theravada Buddhists do not include them in their canon.

words.d: "great vehicle"; the branch of Buddhism common in East Asia and Tibet
a famous Mahayana sutra, much loved in China and Japan

look.title: Big Buddhist Collections
look.cite: Taisho Shinshu Daizokyo; Derge Kangyur; Thai Siamrath Tipitaka
look.prompt: Why might these collections have different sizes?

check.q: What does Mahayana mean?
check.why: Mahayana means great vehicle.

check.q: Which is a Mahayana sutra?
check.why: The Lotus Sutra is a Mahayana sutra. The others are in the Pali Canon.

check.q: Where do many Mahayana sutras survive?
check.why: Many Sanskrit originals were lost, but Chinese and Tibetan translations survive.

lessons.title: No Single Buddhist Bible
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism has no one book that every Buddhist uses; different traditions keep different collections.
reading: Some religions have one main book. Buddhism is different. Buddhists have a large library of scriptures. Different traditions choose different parts. The library is very big.
A Theravada monk in Thailand reads the Pali Canon. A Zen teacher in Japan may chant the Heart Sutra. A Tibetan nun studies texts in the Kangyur. Each is reading Buddhist scripture.
Many families also have favorite texts. A Pure Land Buddhist may love a sutra about Amitabha Buddha. A Nichiren Buddhist chants the name of the Lotus Sutra. No one book holds it all.

words.d: a writing a religion treats as sacred
a branch or way of practice passed down over time

look.title: Three Readers
look.text: A monk in Bangkok opens a Pali book. A teacher in Kyoto chants the Heart Sutra. A nun in Dharamsala unwraps a long Tibetan page. All three are reading Buddhist scriptures.
look.prompt: What is the same and what is different about these three readers?

check.q: Does Buddhism have one book every Buddhist uses?
choices: no, it has a large library
check.why: Buddhism has many scriptures, and traditions choose different parts.

check.q: Which text might a Zen teacher in Japan chant?
check.why: The Heart Sutra is often chanted in Zen temples.

check.q: What is a scripture?
choices: a writing a religion treats as sacred
check.why: A scripture is a writing a religion treats as sacred.

lessons.title: Where the Branches Live
lessons.mainIdea: Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism grew strong in different parts of Asia and now live in America too.
reading: Theravada Buddhism is strongest in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Mahayana Buddhism grew in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam. *Vajrayana* Buddhism is strongest in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia.
Each branch has its own favorite scriptures. Each has its own ways of practice. Buddhists in each branch see themselves as following the Buddha. None is ranked above the others here.
All three branches are found in Illinois today. Families from Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Tibet and many other places have temples here. The Buddhist Temple of Chicago was founded in 1944.

words.d: "way of the elders"; the branch of Buddhism using the Pali Canon
"diamond vehicle"; the branch of Buddhism common in Tibet and Mongolia

look.title: A Map of Branches
look.text: Picture a map of Asia with three colors. One color covers Sri Lanka and Thailand. One covers China, Korea and Japan. One covers Tibet and Mongolia. Now picture dots on Chicago for all three.
look.prompt: What does the Chicago part of the map show?

check.q: Where is Theravada Buddhism strongest?
check.why: Theravada is strongest in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

check.q: What does Vajrayana mean?
check.why: Vajrayana means diamond vehicle. Theravada means way of the elders.

check.q: When was the Buddhist Temple of Chicago founded?
check.why: The Buddhist Temple of Chicago was founded in 1944.

review.q: What are the three baskets of the Tipitaka?
review.why: The three baskets are the Vinaya, the Suttas and the Abhidhamma.

review.q: Which basket holds rules for monks and nuns?
review.why: The Vinaya holds the monastic rules.

review.q: The Dhammapada and the Jatakas belong to which basket?
review.why: Both are in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta basket.

review.q: How many chapters does the Dhammapada have?
review.why: The Dhammapada has 26 chapters and 423 verses.

review.q: What words usually open a sutta?
review.why: Suttas open with evam me sutam, "Thus have I heard."

review.q: Which of these is NOT in the Pali Canon?
review.why: The Lotus Sutra is a Mahayana sutra, not part of the Pali Canon.
The Abhidhamma sorts ideas about the mind into lists.

review.q: Why do people say Buddhism has no single Bible?
review.why: Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhists each treasure different collections.
